blocks.text: But one objection can be raised: namely, that quails do not fly when the south wind blows. Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Οἱ δὲ ὄρτυγες, ὅταν πέσωσιν, ἐὰν μὲν εὐδία ᾖ βόρειον ᾖ, συνδυάζονταί τε, καὶ ἠρεμοῦσιν. ἐὰν δὲ νότος, χαλεπῶς ἔχουσι, διὰ τὸ μὴ εἶναι πτητικοί· ὑγρὸς γὰρ καὶ βαρὺς ὁ ἄνεμος· διὸ καὶ οἱ θηρεύοντες ἐπιχειροῦσι τοῖς νοτίοις· [Hoi de ortyges, hotan pesōsin, ean men eudia ē boreion ē, syndyazontai te, kai ēremousin. ean de notos, chalepōs echousi, dia to mē einai ptētikoi; hygros gar kai barys ho anemos; dio kai hoi thēreuontes epicheirousi tois notiois] "When quails fall (rather, ὅταν πέτονται [hotan petontai], when they fly), if the sky is clear and the wind is from the north, they pair and stay quiet. But if the south wind blows, they fare badly, because they do not fly easily; for that wind is moist and heavy. That is why fowlers go after them when the winds are southerly." And Pliny, book 10, chapter 23: "They do not fly with the south wind, that is, a moist and heavy wind. Yet they want to be carried by a breeze, because of the weight of their bodies and their small strength," etc. "Thus they fly most with the north wind." And Solinus: "They never set out with the south wind, for they fear the force of its swollen blast. They entrust themselves mostly to the north winds, so that a drier and stronger breath may more easily carry forward their rather fat and therefore sluggish bodies." To the same effect is the fact that the winds called Ornithiae, as if they brought birds, are described as blowing from the north, or at least from the west. Aristotle, in the book De mundo: Οἱ δὲ ὀρνιθίαι καλούμενοι, ἐαρινοί τινες ὄντες ἄνεμοι, βόρειοί εἰσι τῷ γένει [Hoi de ornithiai kaloumenoi, earinoi tines ontes anemoi, boreioi eisi tō genei]. Budaeus rendered this: "Certain winds of the northern kind, gaining strength in springtime, are called Ornithiae, as it were 'bird-winds'." But Apuleius quite differently: "The spring Ornithiae (others read winds) are a kind of north wind, issuing from the air with lesser force and not maintaining their blowing with continuous persistence." These words, indeed, are taken not so much from this passage as from the Meteorologica, book 2, chapter 5, where the Ornithiae are said to be Ἐτησίαι ἀσθενεῖς· ἐλάττους δὲ, καὶ ὀψιαίτεροι τῶν Ἐτησίων πνέοντες [Etēsiai astheneis; elattous de, kai opsiaiteroi tōn Etēsiōn pneontes], "weak Etesians, but smaller and later than the true Etesians." In these words the Ornithiae are assigned to the Etesians. The Etesians, however, blow either from the western quarter or from the northern region. Diodorus, book 1: Τοὺς Ἐτησίας ἰδεῖν ἐστιν οὐδέν τι μᾶλλον ἀπὸ τῆς ἄρκτου [II, 666] πνέοντας, ἤπερ τῆς ἑσπέρας· οὐ βορέαι γὰρ, οὐδ᾽ ἀπαρκτίαι μόνοι, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ πνέοντες ἀπὸ τῆς θηρινῆς δύσεως ἀργέσαι κοινωνοῦσι τῆς τῶν Ἐτησίων προσηγορίας [Tous Etēsias idein estin ouden ti mallon apo tēs arktou pneontas, ēper tēs hesperas; ou boreai gar, oud' aparktiai monoi, alla kai hoi pneontes apo tēs thērinēs dyseōs argesai koinōnousi tēs tōn Etēsiōn prosēgorias]. So the Ornithiae arise from the same quarter. And Pliny, book 2, chapter 47, relates them now to the Favonius, now to the Etesians. "Some," he says, "call the Favonius around the 7th day before the Kalends of March Chelidonias, from the sighting of the swallow. [col. 104] Some, however, call it Ornithias, blowing on the 71st day after the winter solstice, from the arrival of the birds, for nine days." And further on, concerning the Etesians: "There also blow after the winter solstice those called Ornithiae, but gentler, and for a few days." In Aristophanes' Acharnians χειμὼν ὀρνιθίας [cheimōn ornithias] is taken otherwise, namely for a most bitterly cold winter, in which τὰ ὄρνεα διαφθείρεται [ta ornea diaphtheiretai], birds perish from the cold, as the Scholiast and Suidas under the word Ὀρνιθίας [Ornithias] hold. Accordingly, for them the ὀρνιθίας [ornithias] wind is ὁ ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν τὰ ὄρνεα στρωννὺς ὑπὸ τῆς ψυχρᾶς πνοῆς [ho epi tēn gēn ta ornea strōnnys hypo tēs psychras pnoēs], "the one that lays birds low on the ground with its cold blast." But for the philosophers the Ornithias wind is nothing other than what we have said, namely a wind bringing birds from the north or the west. It might therefore seem that it happened contrary to nature that the south wind carried the quails to the Israelites. And from this very point some argue that the miracle was greater. But there is no need to resort to this. For although Pliny and Solinus flatly deny that they fly with the south wind, from the Philosopher you can draw only this: that they then fly with more difficulty and are more easily caught ^{(8)}.
